title: requestAnimationFrame (V-Sync)
concept: requestAnimationFrame (rAF) runs your code in sync with the browser's screen refresh cycle (V-Sync).

steps.title: Starting the animation
steps.explanation:
Calling `requestAnimationFrame(goodAni)` to start the animation loop.
This is like telling the browser: "Run `goodAni` right before you draw the next frame."
steps.keyInsight: rAF aligns work to the browser's rendering cycle, not a fixed time interval.

steps.title: Scheduling the next frame
steps.explanation:
Inside `goodAni`, we call `requestAnimationFrame(goodAni)` again to schedule the next frame.
This is the 'rAF loop' — the key to smooth animations.

steps.title: Note: the wrong way — using setTimeout
steps.explanation:
Using `setTimeout` like in `badAni` can misalign JS execution with the browser's rendering cycle.
For example, if `moveBox` runs right after a render finishes, the result won't appear until the next frame 16ms later — causing the choppy 'Jank' effect.
steps.keyInsight: For JS animations, always use `requestAnimationFrame` instead of `setTimeout`.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT a key feature of requestAnimationFrame?
options: It pauses in background tabs to save battery
Call frequency automatically adjusts to the monitor's refresh rate (Hz)
It's effective at reducing frame drops (Jank)
quiz.explanation:
rAF follows the screen refresh cycle, not a fixed time.
The interval varies dynamically based on the display environment.

misconceptions.wrong: JS animations (rAF) are always faster than CSS animations
misconceptions.why:
For simple movements, CSS can be faster because it runs off the main thread on the Compositor Thread.
rAF is for cases that need complex calculations, like physics engines.

keyTakeaway: JS animations must use rAF to stay in sync with V-Sync for smooth rendering.
